Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
Being reminded of the event by others

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I can't deal with even the slightest upset

vignette:
Imani had been a tutor for over a decade, finding quiet satisfaction in the small, ordered world of algebra problems and essay structures. That world shattered six months ago. Walking home from a late session, a man had pulled her into a dark alcove between two apartment buildings. The assault was a blur of violence and powerlessness, a chaotic vortex of sensations that refused to coalesce into a linear story. Throughout the attack, the sound of a small child crying hysterically echoed from an open window somewhere above, a sound that became inextricably woven into the fabric of the trauma. The physical violation left her with a deep, sickening nausea that felt as much a part of the memory as the violence itself.

In the weeks that followed, the event refused to settle into the past. For Imani, the memory itself felt like a foreign object lodged in her mind; it didn't feel like something that had happened to her, but rather a silent, terrifying film she was forced to watch, starring someone else (Memory Feels Alien). When fragments did surface—the rough texture of a brick wall against her back, the crying from the window—they brought with them the same undiluted terror she had felt that night, a primal fear that left her breathless and trembling (Terror on Recall). This wordless, sensory nature of the memory began to dictate her reality. The sound of any child crying, even in a distant playground, would plunge her back into that state of alert, and a simple wave of nausea could trigger a cascade of panic (Memory → Triggers). The sheer horror of these fragments, and her inability to articulate them, solidified a devastating belief: something inside her had been fundamentally broken by the attack, and she was now permanently changed for the worse (Memory → Negative Appraisals).

This conviction that she was too damaged to function governed every choice she made. Believing she could not handle even the slightest upset, she began to dismantle her life as a form of self-protection (Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies). She started turning down invitations from her partner, especially for things that might make her happy, like a favorite restaurant or a walk in the park. Joy felt reckless, an open invitation for more pain. When her partner would gently ask how she was doing, she would offer a clipped "I'm fine," terrified that being reminded of the event would cause her to completely unravel (Thought Avoidance). This avoidance was fueled directly by the terror of the memory itself; she would do anything to keep those silent, horrifying images at bay (Memory → Maladaptive Strategies).

Her work, once a source of stability, became a minefield. During a session last week, her student’s younger brother began to wail in the next room. The sound instantly triggered a cold sweat and a familiar roiling in her stomach. For Imani, this wasn't just a distressing noise; it was confirmation of her deepest fears. It proved she was unsafe, fragile, and utterly incapable of managing her own life (Triggers → Negative Appraisals). She had to end the session abruptly, inventing a sudden migraine, overwhelmed by a sense of shame at her own perceived weakness. The uncertainty of when a trigger might strike next left her in a constant state of low-grade dread.

In the quiet hours after such an incident, her mind would turn inward, relentlessly replaying not the assault, but her own supposed failures. She would spend hours blaming herself for walking home alone, for not screaming louder, for simply being there (Self-Blame). This rumination did not provide answers; it only kept the trauma alive, preventing the memory from ever being processed or integrated (Maladaptive Strategies → Memory). Each cycle of avoidance and self-blame reinforced her belief that she was irreparably damaged and unable to cope, a conclusion that felt more true with every social event she missed and every tutoring session she dreaded (Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals). The more she retreated from the world to avoid reminders, the more her sensitivity to them grew, making the triggers feel even more potent when they inevitably found her (Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers).

The breaking point came when the parents of the student she had left abruptly called to say they would not be continuing her services, citing her recent unreliability. The loss of her job, combined with the growing strain in her relationship, made her fear of complete collapse feel terrifyingly real. Imani sought therapy not with any sense of hope, but out of a final, desperate act of preservation. She remains convinced that talking about what happened will destroy her, but she is now even more afraid of the silent, shrinking world her avoidance has built.
